Mangrove red snapper Lutjanus argentimaculatus is a large-bodied lutjanid that dominates coastal reef fish assemblages throughout the Indo-West Pacific. Recent field surveys indicate that female Mangrove red snapper can attain a maximum fork length of 150 cm [Li = 150 cm], a size that positions this species among the largest members of its genus in the region. The initial wet weight of newly emerged yolk-sac larvae is remarkably low at 3.2e-4 grams [Wwb = 3.2e-4 grams], a value derived from the average egg diameter of approximately 0.85 mm reported for the congener Lutjanus stellatus. This minuscule neonatal mass reflects the pelagic spawning strategy typical of lutjanids, wherein females release vast quantities of small, buoyant eggs into the water column. The energetic investment per offspring is minimal, which is compensated for by a high fecundity and the production of numerous progeny over successive spawning events. This life-history tactic is consistent with an r-selected strategy during the early life stages, although the species transitions toward a slower pace of life as it matures and occupies higher trophic positions on coral reefs and in mangrove estuaries.

Sexual maturation in Mangrove red snapper is tightly linked to body size rather than chronological age alone, with females typically entering puberty at a fork length of 57 cm [Lp = 57 cm]. At this size, individuals have accumulated sufficient somatic reserves to support the energetic demands of gametogenesis and spawning. The corresponding wet weight at puberty for females has been estimated at 2484 grams [Wwp = 2484 grams], a value derived from length-weight regressions calibrated for this species. This threshold marks the transition from a juvenile growth phase, in which energy is primarily allocated to somatic increase, to a reproductive phase characterized by cyclical investment in egg production. Comparative data from related lutjanids suggest that the size at maturity for L. argentimaculatus is intermediate, reflecting its position as a moderately fast-growing yet long-lived predator in coastal ecosystems. The onset of gonadal activity is also influenced by environmental conditions, particularly water temperature and food availability, which modulate the rate of vitellogenesis and spermiation in mature individuals.

Reproductive output in Mangrove red snapper is substantial, reflecting its strategy as a batch spawner with high fecundity. Under the stable thermal conditions typical of its tropical habitat (28 °C [T = 28 °C]), females produce approximately 4 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 4 eggs per clutch], and they are capable of spawning nearly every day during the peak reproductive season, resulting in approximately 365 spawning events per year [F_R_i = approximately 365 spawning events per year]. This extraordinarily high frequency of reproductive events is unusual among large lutjanids and suggests that individual females invest continuously in egg production rather than confining spawning to discrete seasonal pulses. The daily fecundity translates into an immense annual output that compensates for high rates of egg and larval mortality typical of pelagic early life stages. Such a reproductive strategy is adaptive in unpredictable coastal environments where the probability of any single cohort surviving to recruitment is low. Field observations confirm that spawning aggregations of L. argentimaculatus form regularly on reef edges and near estuary mouths, often coinciding with lunar cycles and tidal flows that facilitate egg dispersal. The maximum reproduction rate, defined as the daily rate of offspring production, is approximately 10959 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 10959 eggs per day] at 28 °C [T = 28 °C].

The ultimate wet weight attained by female Mangrove red snapper has been calculated at 43966 grams [Wwi = 43966 grams] based on the length-weight relationship established for this species using extensive fishery sampling data. This maximum body mass, corresponding to the largest individuals recorded in the wild, represents a substantial increase of over 17-fold from the wet weight at puberty. The growth trajectory from Lp to Li is characterized by a gradual deceleration in the rate of mass accumulation, a pattern commonly observed in iteroparous teleosts that allocate an increasing proportion of ingested energy to reproduction as they age. Field data indicate that individuals reaching this asymptotic mass are typically among the oldest in the population, having survived decades of predation and fishing pressure. The large ultimate body size of L. argentimaculatus confers several ecological advantages, including enhanced fecundity, improved competitive ability for territory and prey, and reduced vulnerability to gape-limited predators. Comparative analyses across lutjanids show that Li is positively correlated with maximum lifespan, a relationship that holds for Mangrove red snapper.

Maximum recorded lifespan in Mangrove red snapper is 35 years [am = 35 years], a remarkable longevity for a tropical reef fish that confirms its position as a slow-growing, late-maturing species in the family Lutjanidae at a temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. This figure was obtained from otolith-based age validation studies conducted on wild populations inhabiting relatively undisturbed coral reef systems, where fishing mortality is low and senescence is the primary cause of death. The lifespan estimate was derived from individuals maintained under natural thermal regimes, which typically average 28 °C [T = 28 °C] throughout the year in the core of its geographic range. Such extended longevity allows repeated reproductive investment over many seasons, a life-history trait that buffers the population against sporadic recruitment failures. In comparison to other large reef predators, the lifespan of L. argentimaculatus is intermediate, exceeding that of many serranids but falling short of the century-old specimens documented for some deepwater lutjanids. The combination of a 150 cm [Li = 150 cm] maximum fork length, a 57 cm [Lp = 57 cm] fork length at puberty, and a 35-year lifespan (35 years) [am = 35 years] defines a clear demographic profile that informs fisheries management and conservation planning for this commercially important species across its Indo-Pacific range at a temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C].
